executive_thesis:
Part V brings the entire Codex to its metaphysical and epistemological summit by uniting five foundational lectures from St. Thomas Aquinas's *Sententia super Metaphysicam* (Books V, VII, and IX) with the systematic syntheses of the *Summa Theologiae* (Prima Pars, qq. 7, 12, 84, and 85), *Quaestiones Disputatae de Potentia Dei* (q. 7, a. 2), and *Quaestiones Disputatae de Veritate* (q. 10, a. 6). Whereas Parts I through IV charted the division of the speculative sciences, the apodictic structure of Euclidean demonstration, the psychological necessity of the spatial phantasm, and the physical ontology of the continuum, Part V grounds all of these doctrines in first philosophy. In *Metaphysics* V, lect. 9, Aquinas distinguishes real categorical being—contracted proportionally according to diverse modes of being (*modi essendi*) and predicating (*modi praedicandi*), with quantity following upon matter as the first intrinsic accident—from propositional being (*esse* as the verbal copula signifying the truth of judgment, illustrated by the falsity of the diagonal's commensurability) and from the division of every category by potency and act (illustrated by the midpoint latent in potency within a continuous line). In *Metaphysics* VII, lect. 10–11, he resolves the Platonic-Pythagorean temptation to reduce geometric figures to pure numbers by establishing the hylomorphic analogy of mathematics: just as natural species require common sensible matter (flesh and bone) in their definition while abstracting from individual sensible matter, mathematical species such as the circle and the right angle dispense with sensible matter (bronze, stone, wood) yet require common *materia intelligibilis* (the continuum, lines, and surfaces) in their universal definition, while individual mathematical circles grasped in pure imagination are individuated by designated intelligible matter and posterior parts such as semicircles.

From the static definition of mathematical essences, *Metaphysics* IX shifts to the dynamic order of actuality and heuristic discovery. In *Metaphysics* IX, lect. 3, Aquinas defends real potentiality against Megarian necessitarianism and Protagorean relativism, establishes the modal law of conditional consequence alongside the impossibility of commensurability between the square's diagonal and side, and formulates the genetic principle that the name and notion of *actus* (*energeia*) are first imposed upon sensible motion—what is first evident to us—and extended thence to higher actualities. In *Metaphysics* IX, lect. 10, this metaphysics of act yields the classical locus on constructive geometric discovery (*inventio*): geometers discover latent truths by dividing lines and surfaces (*dividendo inveniunt*), reducing potential constructions into act so that, once the side of a triangle is produced (Euclid *Elements* I.32) or the radius is drawn from the midpoint of the diameter to the circumference (Euclid *Elements* III.31), the necessary nexus becomes immediately manifest to one inspecting the figure (*statim manifestum fit videnti dispositionem figurae*). The systematic articles in *Summa Theologiae* I, q. 84, a. 6–7, q. 85, a. 1, and *De Veritate* q. 10, a. 6 supply the complete cognitive architecture of this insight: steering an Aristotelian middle course between Democritean materialism and Platonic-Avicennian extrinsicism, Aquinas demonstrates that phantasms serve as the *materia causae* and instrumental agent under the principal light of the *intellectus agens*, that actual understanding always requires *conversio ad phantasmata* to behold the universal nature in the particular exemplar, and that abstraction by simple and absolute consideration isolates mathematical quantity in *materia intelligibilis communis* without mendacity while implanting the habit of first indemonstrable principles.

Finally, *Summa Theologiae* I, q. 7, a. 1 and 3, q. 12, a. 4, and *De Potentia* q. 7, a. 2 crown the Codex with Aquinas's existential metaphysics of *ipsum esse*. Contrasting the privative infinity of quantitative division—which approaches matter and underpins the geometer's operational *linea infinita*—against the formal perfection of unreceived act, Aquinas declares that *esse* itself is most formal of all (*maxime formale omnium*) and, in the celebrated formula of *De Potentia* q. 7, a. 2, ad 9, *the actuality of all acts and on account of this the perfection of all perfections* (*actualitas omnium actuum, et propter hoc perfectio omnium perfectionum*). Because the human intellect can consider in abstraction what it knows in concretion (*ST* I, q. 12, a. 4, ad 3), resolving concrete composites into both form and *esse*, it grasps diverse proportional modes of being and affirms objective existential and formal nexuses in judgment. As Peter Hoenen S.J. demonstrated across *La théorie du jugement d'après St. Thomas d'Aquin* (1946) and *De Noetica Geometriae* (1954)—paralleled by Bernard Lonergan's *Verbum* (1967)—and as the GEOMETOR ecosystem realizes computationally across *geometor.model*, *geometor.explorer*, and *geometor.divine*, geometric construction in act is the privileged arena where human intelligence experiences pre-judgmental insight into necessary nexus within intelligible matter before sealing that discovery in rational judgment.

conceptual_table.english_term: Modes of being and modes of predicating
conceptual_table.significance: Establishes that *ens* is not a genus contracted by extrinsic differences, but analogically diversified into ten categories proportional to real modes of inherence, with quantity following intrinsically upon matter.

conceptual_table.locus: Metaph. V, lect. 9; De Pot. q. 7, a. 2, ad 1
conceptual_table.significance: Distinguishes the existential and categorical act of being in reality from the copulative *est* formed by the composing and dividing intellect to signify that an affirmation or negation—including mathematical impossibility or privation—is true.

conceptual_table.locus: Metaph. VII, lect. 10–11; ST I, q. 85, a. 1, ad 2
conceptual_table.significance: Defines substance insofar as it underlies pure continuous extension apart from sensible qualities: common intelligible matter (the continuum, lines, surfaces) enters universal geometric definitions, whereas individual intelligible matter individuates particular diagrams in imagination.

Illustrates why sensible substrates (bronze, wood, stone) are excluded from geometric essences, yet plurality of equal lines and similar circles in pure *phantasia* proves that mathematical objects retain individual intelligible matter.

Explains why the name and intelligible conception of *actus* (*energeia* and *entelecheia*) originate from local and qualitative motion—the actuality most manifest to sense—and are analogically extended to immutable forms, intellectual operations, and *esse*.

conceptual_table.english_term: Geometric discovery by division in act
conceptual_table.significance: Reveals the heuristic mechanism of constructive geometry: drawing auxiliary lines and circles actualizes divisions previously latent in the continuum's potency, making demonstrative middle terms immediately visible in the diagram.

conceptual_table.locus: ST I, q. 7, a. 3, arg. 1 & ad 1
conceptual_table.significance: Clarifies that Euclidean geometry never posits an actually infinite magnitude, which would violate the terminating nature of *figura*, but uses 'infinite line' operationally for an arbitrarily extensible finite segment.

conceptual_table.english_term: Resolution of the concrete in abstraction
conceptual_table.significance: Identifies the distinctive mark elevating intellect above sense: whereas sight perceives nature only as *this* concrete singular, created intellect resolves composites so as to consider both concrete form and concrete *esse* in abstraction.

conceptual_table.english_term: Matter of the cause / instrumental agent
conceptual_table.locus: ST I, q. 84, a. 6; De Ver. q. 10, a. 6, ad 7
conceptual_table.significance: Synthesizes sensory empiricism and intellectual immateriality: phantasms act as secondary, instrumental causes supplying determinate structural content, while the *intellectus agens* acts as principal cause conferring actual intelligibility.

Demonstrates that even after abstracting habitual intelligible species, the embodied human intellect must turn to exemplar phantasms to inspect the universal nature existing in the particular—the exact psychological law governing mathematical diagrams.

conceptual_table.english_term: Abstraction by simple and absolute consideration
conceptual_table.significance: Vindicates the truth of mathematics against Platonic hypostatization: considering quantity and figure without considering sensible qualities involves no false judgment of separation, because the mode of understanding follows the knower rather than the mode of material existence.

conceptual_table.english_term: Being itself, the actuality of all acts
conceptual_table.locus: ST I, q. 7, a. 1; De Pot. q. 7, a. 2, ad 9
conceptual_table.significance: Establishes *esse* not as an empty genus or minimal substrate, but as the ultimate formal perfection actualizing every substantial and accidental form, contracted by quidditative potency in creatures and subsisting unreceived in God.

section_summaries.heading: Metaphysics Book V, Lecture 9 — On the Division of Per Se Being into Ten Categories and Being Signified by Propositional Judgment
section_summaries.argument_summary: Commenting on Aristotle's philosophical lexicon (*Metaphysics* Δ.7, 1017a7–b9), Aquinas distinguishes *ens per accidens* (accidental predication across a common subject) from *ens per se*, which he subdivides into three fundamental orders: first, extramental *ens perfectum* contracted proportionally into the ten categories according to diverse modes of predicating that track diverse modes of being (correcting Avicenna's claim that accidental terms primarily signify substance); second, intramental *esse* signified by the verbal copula of propositional composition and division, which expresses the truth of a statement as effect to extramental cause (illustrated by privations like blindness and the negation of the diagonal's commensurability with the side of a square); and third, the division of all categories by potency and act, illustrated by the statue of Mercury in stone and the midpoint latent in potency within a continuous line.
key_theses: Being (*ens*) cannot be a genus contracted by extrinsic differences, because nothing lies outside being; instead, it contracts into the ten categories proportionally as *modi praedicandi* follow real *modi essendi*.
Quantity inheres in substance *per se* and absolutely as consequent upon matter, whereas quality follows upon form and relation regards another.

Propositional *esse* formed by the composing and dividing intellect signifies that a statement is true (*quia aliquod dictum est verum*), extending even to privations and mathematical impossibilities such as the incommensurability of the square's diagonal.
Every category is divided by act and potency, just as every part of a continuum—such as the midpoint of a line—exists potentially in the whole prior to actual division.

section_summaries.heading: Metaphysics Book VII, Lecture 10 — On Parts of the Form vs. Parts of Matter: Bronze Circle and Mathematical Circle in Intelligible Matter
section_summaries.argument_summary: Expositing *Metaphysics* Z.10 (1034b20–1036a25), Aquinas resolves whether the parts of a whole are prior to the whole and enter its definition. He distinguishes parts of the form or *ratio*—which are prior to the composite and belong to the universal definition—from parts into which the concrete whole divides as into matter, which are posterior. Thus the acute angle is defined through the right angle and the semicircle through the circle, not conversely. Crucially, Aquinas distinguishes universal composites (which include common matter) from singular composites individuated by designated matter—not only sensible singulars (bronze or wooden circles) but also mathematical singulars (plural equal lines and similar circles grasped by pure *phantasia*), which are individuated by *materia intelligibilis* (the continuum, surface, or body) and cannot be defined as singulars once they recede from actual inspection.
key_theses: Formal parts belong to the *quod quid erat esse* and are prior to the defined whole, whereas material parts into which a figure is divided—such as the acute angle relative to the right angle or the semicircle relative to the circle—are posterior to the form and defined through it.

Definition belongs solely to the universal species, never to singulars, whether sensible (a bronze circle) or mathematical (this imagined circle), because matter in itself is unknowable save through the universal form.

Plurality within a single mathematical species—such as multiple equal lines or multiple similar figures—proves the existence of mathematical singulars apprehended apart from external sense by *phantasia* alone.

Intelligible matter (*materia intelligibilis*) exists in sensible things not insofar as they are sensible, but insofar as they are continuous magnitudes (continuum, surface, or three-dimensional body) underlying mathematical forms.

section_summaries.heading: Metaphysics Book VII, Lecture 11 — How Mathematical Species Are Defined Without Sensible Matter Yet Not Without Common Intelligible Matter
section_summaries.argument_summary: Continuing into *Metaphysics* Z.11 (1036a26–1037b7), Aquinas confronts the Platonic and Pythagorean error—including the misleading 'parable of Socrates the Younger'—which argued that just as bronze forms no part of the circle's essence, neither should flesh and bone belong to human essence nor continuous lines to the essence of the triangle and circle, thereby reducing all mathematical species to pure numbers (such as the dyad for the straight line). Aquinas refutes this hyper-formalism by showing it collapses diverse species sharing a number (a three-sided triangle, a three-term syllogism, a three-dimensional body) into a single species and ultimately reduces all reality to bare unity. Against this, he establishes that mathematical definitions exclude all sensible matter yet must retain common intelligible matter (lines and the continuum), while excluding individual intelligible matter (these particular lines or semicircles), so that only pure immaterial substances are wholly identical in reality with their *quod quid erat esse*.
key_theses: Eliminating intelligible matter (the continuum and lines) from geometric definitions reduces triangles and circles to abstract numbers, absurdly identifying a triangle (three lines), a syllogism (three terms), and a body (three dimensions) in species.

The 'parable of Socrates the Younger' errs by equating the relation of man to flesh and bone with that of a circle to bronze: natural species require sensible organs ordered to motion, whereas mathematical species abstract from sensible matter while retaining proportionate intelligible matter.

Semicircles are excluded from the universal definition of the circle not because they are sensible like bronze, but because they are material parts of singular circles in individual intelligible matter rather than formal parts of the universal species.

In extramental reality, any substance composed with matter—even if considered logically as universal—differs in the concrete individual from its abstract quiddity; only separate subsistent forms are strictly identical with their *quod quid erat esse*.

section_summaries.heading: Metaphysics Book IX, Lecture 3 — How the Name and Notion of Actuality Are Derived First from Sensible Motion
section_summaries.argument_summary: Commenting on *Metaphysics* Θ.3–4 (1046b29–1047b30), Aquinas first refutes the Megarian thesis that potency exists only when acting—showing that it abolishes habitual art and geometry, resurrects Protagorean subjectivism regarding sensible qualities, and destroys all motion and generation—and then refutes the opposite extreme that everything is possible even if impossible consequences follow, citing the geometric impossibility of the square's diagonal being commensurable with its side. Between these extremes, he defines the possible as that from whose supposition nothing impossible follows, demonstrates the modal theorem that a possible antecedent in a valid conditional entails a possible consequent, and articulates the foundational epistemological principle that because names signify intelligible conceptions and we name first what we understand first, the name and notion of *actus* (*energeia*) were first imposed upon sensible motion and thence derived to form, operation, and existence.
key_theses: Collapsing potency into act abolishes habitual science and art, reduces sensible qualities to Protagorean appearances, and renders all generation and transition impossible.

Falsehood differs radically from impossibility: that Socrates stands when seated is contingently false yet possible, whereas the commensurability of a square's diagonal with its side is both false and intrinsically impossible because positing it entails contradiction.

Since spoken names follow the order of human understanding rather than the order of nature, the concept and term *actus* are first grasped in sensible motion—the actuality most evident to us—and extended analogically to immutable actualities.
In any valid conditional *if A, then B*, taking *possible* as opposed to *impossible*, the possibility of the antecedent *A* necessarily entails the possibility of the consequent *B*.

section_summaries.heading: Metaphysics Book IX, Lecture 10 — On Discovering Geometric Truth by Dividing Figures in Act (Euclid I.32 and III.31)
section_summaries.argument_summary: Expositing *Metaphysics* Θ.9 (1051a4–33), Aquinas first shows why actuality is better than potency in good things (and worse in evils, excluding evil and corruption from eternal beings lacking potency) and then delivers the locus classicus of the entire Aristotelian-Thomistic tradition on geometric discovery (*inventio*). Geometric diagrams (*diagrammata*) are discovered in truth by dividing lines and surfaces in act (*dividendo inveniunt*). Because the parts and auxiliary relations of a continuum lie only in potency when a figure is first drawn, the sought theorem remains hidden; once the geometer actualizes those divisions—by extending the base of a triangle to form the exterior angle (Euclid I.32) or by bisecting the diameter at the center and drawing the radius to the vertex on the semicircle (Euclid III.31)—the conclusion becomes immediately manifest to one inspecting the figure, because the intellect itself is act and understands things insofar as they are brought into act.
key_theses: Geometers discover sought truths by dividing lines and surfaces, reducing into act structural relations that were merely latent in potency in the initial drawing of the figure.

In Euclid *Elements* I.32, producing side *AC* of triangle *ABC* actualizes the exterior angle at *C*, making it immediately evident (*statim manifestum*) from the equality of adjacent angles to two right angles that the interior angles equal two right angles.

In Euclid *Elements* III.31, dividing diameter *AC* at center *D* and drawing radius *DB* actualizes three equal radii (*DA*, *DC*, *DB*) and two isosceles triangles, rendering it immediately manifest to one who knows the principles of geometry that every angle inscribed in a semicircle is right.

Truth is discovered when potentiality is reduced to act because the intellect is itself act, and what is understood must exist in act—hence 'by making something in act, geometers know' (*facientes aliquid actu cognoscunt*).

section_summaries.heading: Summa Theologiae I, q. 7, a. 1 & a. 3; q. 12, a. 4 — Being Itself as Most Formal of All; the Geometer's Infinite Line; Apprehending Absolute Being
section_summaries.argument_summary: These three articles from the Prima Pars establish the metaphysical polarity between quantitative limitation and subsistent *esse*, together with the abstractive power of created intellect. In Question 7, Article 1, Aquinas distinguishes imperfect material infinity (formless indeterminacy) from perfect formal infinity, proving that because *ipsum esse* is most formal of all (*maxime formale omnium*), God as unreceived subsistent being is infinito-perfect, whereas figure is the quantitative boundary terminating extension. In Question 7, Article 3, he proves that neither a natural body nor an actually imagined mathematical body can be infinite in magnitude because every actual mathematical body must have a terminating figure, explaining that the geometer's 'infinite line' means only a finite line extensible or subtractable as needed, and that quantitative infinity belongs solely to division toward matter, never addition toward the formal whole. In Question 12, Article 4, he maps the hierarchy of cognitive powers to modes of being and demonstrates in the third reply that because the human intellect can resolve concrete composites to consider form and *esse* in abstraction, it possesses a natural openness to being elevated by grace.
key_theses: Matter is perfected and made finite by form, whereas form's amplitude is contracted by matter; because *ipsum esse* is most formal of all, unreceived subsistent *esse* is supremely infinite and perfect.

No mathematical body can exist in act without some figure (*figura*), which is the form of quantity enclosed by boundaries; hence an actually infinite magnitude is impossible both physically and mathematically.

When the geometer postulates 'Let this line be infinite,' he requires no actually infinite line, but only an actually finite line from which as much may be taken as demonstration requires; quantitative infinity exists solely in potential division toward matter.

Unlike bodily sight, which grasps nature solely in concrete singularity, created intellect resolves what is concrete so as to consider both form and *esse* in abstraction (*per modum resolutionis cuiusdam*).

section_summaries.heading: Summa Theologiae I, q. 84, a. 6–7 & q. 85, a. 1 — On the Origin of Science from Sensible Things, Turning to Phantasms, and Threefold Abstraction
section_summaries.argument_summary: In the Treatise on Man, Aquinas delivers his definitive account of human intellectual cognition. Question 84, Article 6 traces an Aristotelian middle path between Democritus (who reduced intellect to passive sensory effluxes) and Plato (who severed intellect from sense via participation in separate Forms): sense operates in the psychophysical composite, while the incorporeal *intellectus agens* renders sensory phantasms intelligible in act, making sensible cognition not the total cause of science, but the *materia causae*. Question 84, Article 7 proves from organ lesions and universal introspection—forming exemplary diagrams whenever we strive to understand or teach—that the embodied intellect cannot understand anything in act, even habitual science, without *conversio ad phantasmata* to behold the universal nature existing in the particular. Question 85, Article 1 refutes the charge that abstraction falsifies reality by distinguishing abstraction via judgmental separation from abstraction via simple consideration, and articulates the canonical hierarchy of individual/common sensible matter and individual/common intelligible matter across physics, mathematics, and metaphysics.
key_theses: Sensible cognition is neither the total efficient cause of intellectual science (Democritus) nor a mere extrinsic occasion awakening innate Ideas (Plato), but serves as the *materia causae* rendered intelligible in act by the *intellectus agens*.

Even after acquiring habitual science, the human intellect in this life cannot understand anything in act without *conversio ad phantasmata*, forming exemplary phantasms in which it inspects the universal nature existing in the particular.

Abstraction by simple and absolute consideration involves no mendacity (*abstrahentium non est mendacium*), because considering specific or quantitative nature apart from individuating conditions reflects the immaterial mode of the knower rather than asserting real separation in the thing.

Physics abstracts from individual sensible matter while retaining common sensible matter; mathematics abstracts from all sensible matter and from individual intelligible matter while retaining common intelligible matter (substance subject to quantity); metaphysics abstracts even from common intelligible matter.

section_summaries.heading: Disputed Questions on the Power of God, q. 7, a. 2 — That Esse Is the Actuality of All Acts and the Perfection of All Perfections
section_summaries.argument_summary: Addressing eleven incisive objections against the identity of essence and *esse* in God, Aquinas constructs a rigorous causal and metaphysical demonstration. Because all created causes, despite differing in their proper specific effects (fire generating fire, a builder building a house), concur in one universal effect—causing *esse*—that common effect must derive from the highest universal cause whose own proper nature is *esse* itself. In the replies, Aquinas deploys the distinction between substantive *esse* and propositional *esse* (*Metaph.* V.9) to explain how we know *that* God is without knowing *what* He is (ad 1); distinguishes *ens commune* (abstraction without precision, open to addition) from *esse divinum* (subsistent purity excluding all addition, ad 6); distinguishes *id quod significatur* from our concrete *modus significandi* (ad 7); explains why 'God is' is self-evident in itself—like *Every whole is greater than its part*—yet demonstrable *quoad nos* (ad 11); and crowns the article in ad 9 by proclaiming *hoc quod dico esse* to be the actuality of all acts and the perfection of all perfections, determined by quidditative natures not as potency by act, but as act by potency.
key_theses: Whereas Damascene's statement that 'that God is, is manifest to us' refers to propositional *esse* conceived by the intellect from effects, God's substantive *actum essendi* is identical with His essence and exceeds natural comprehension.
Common being (*ens commune*) abstracts without excluding further determination, whereas subsistent divine *esse* is individuated by its sheer unreceived purity, excluding any possible addition.

What Aquinas calls *esse* (*hoc quod dico esse*) is the actuality of all acts (*actualitas omnium actuum*) and the perfection of all perfections: no form is understood to exist in act unless *esse* is posited, and *esse* is limited by essence as act is contracted by potency.

Like the axiom *Every whole is greater than its part* for one ignorant of the term 'whole,' the proposition 'God is' is *per se nota secundum se* yet requires *quia* demonstration *quoad nos* because God's quiddity is not directly known to us.

section_summaries.heading: Disputed Questions on Truth, q. 10, a. 6 — Whether the Human Mind Receives Knowledge from Sensible Things and on First Indemonstrable Principles
section_summaries.argument_summary: In this masterly disputed question on the mind (*De Mente*), Aquinas classifies and critiques four historical accounts of the origin of science—two purely extrinsic (Platonic separate Ideas and Avicenna's separate *intelligentia agens*) and two purely intrinsic (Platonic reminiscence from pre-existent souls and radical Augustinian self-formation)—before establishing Aristotle's synthesis that human science arises *partim ab intrinseco et partim ab extrinseco*. Toward external sensible things, our mind stands simultaneously as act to potency (via the *intellectus agens*, whose participated light derives ultimately from God) and as potency to act (via the *intellectus possibilis*, receptive of determinate species). In the light of the agent intellect, all science is originally implanted in us (*originaliter indita*) through universal conceptions—first indemonstrable principles arising from sense (*sed contra* 2)—while in the crucial seventh reply Aquinas formulates the synergy of abstraction: the *intellectus agens* acts as primary principal agent and the phantasms act as secondary instrumental agent, imprinting species in the possible intellect that are both intelligible in act and determinate likenesses of sensible things.
key_theses: All human science originally consists in the knowledge of first indemonstrable principles, whose cognition arises in us from sense (*Posterior Analytics* II.19) under the illuminating light of the agent intellect.

Purely extrinsic theories (Plato, Avicenna) fail to explain why the lack of a bodily sense entails the lack of the corresponding science and why injury to the organ of imagination impedes actual consideration; purely intrinsic theories (pre-existence, pure self-expression) violate the natural hylomorphic union of soul and body.

Human science originates partly from within (the participated light of the *intellectus agens*, wherein universal first principles are immediately known) and partly from without (determinate forms drawn from sensible things).

In intellectual abstraction, the *intellectus agens* operates as principal and primary agent while the phantasms operate as instrumental and secondary agent (*agens instrumentale vel secundarium*), leaving an intelligible species in the possible intellect that bears the imprint of both.

section_notes.heading: Metaphysics Book V, Lecture 9 — On the Division of Per Se Being into Ten Categories and Being Signified by Propositional Judgment
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Aquinas's exposition of *Metaphysics* Δ.7 (1017a7–b9) transforms Aristotle's compact lexical entry into a foundational treatise on analogical predication and the architecture of the categories (paralleled in *In III Physicorum*, lect. 5, in Part IV of this Codex). Against Parmenidean monism and Platonic univocity, Aquinas invokes *Metaphysics* B.3 (998b22) to prove that *ens* cannot be a genus, deriving the ten categories systematically from the triple relation of predicate to subject: essential identity (substance), intrinsic inherence consequent upon matter (quantity), upon form (quality), or toward another (relation), and extrinsic denomination by measure or causal principle/term. Equally decisive is his explicit refutation of Avicenna (*Liber de Philosophia Prima* III.2–4), who treated concrete accidental predicates like *album* as signifying substance primarily and quality secondarily; Aquinas insists that *album* primarily signifies quality in an accidental mode (*esse est inesse*), preserving the integrity of the nine accidental categories—chief among them mathematical quantity—as genuine modes of *ens per se* rather than collapsing them into *ens per accidens*.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Two canonical Euclidean paradigms anchor Lecture 9's distinctions of propositional truth and potentiality. In Marietti n. 895, illustrating how *non esse* signifies the falsity of a proposition, Aquinas explicates Aristotle's famous example (1017a34–35): to say that the diagonal of a square is *not* incommensurable with its side is to assert what is false—alluding to the Pythagorean-Euclidean proof (preserved in *Elements* X, Appendix 27, and implied by *Elements* I.47 and X.9) that the ratio of diagonal to side (√2 : 1) admits no common unit measure. Immediately afterward, in Marietti n. 897, illustrating *ens in potentia* across the categories, Aquinas cites the midpoint of a line (*medium lineae*) as existing potentially within the undivided line (*Elements* I.10 bisects a given finite straight line in act), noting explicitly that Aristotle places the line provisionally among substances in view of the Pythagorean-Platonic thesis not yet refuted in Book V.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In the Appendix to *De Noetica Geometriae* (1954) and throughout *La théorie du jugement d'après St. Thomas d'Aquin* (1946/1953), Peter Hoenen S.J. makes *In V Metaphysicorum*, lect. 9 (especially Marietti nn. 890, 895–896) the cornerstone of his distinction between the two operations of the intellect and the analogical diversity of *esse*. Hoenen highlights Aquinas's guiding principle—*quoties ens dicitur, toties esse significatur*—showing that diverse *modi essendi* (substantial subsistence, quantitative extension, qualitative intensity, fluent motion) originate from the quidditative natures and relations affirmed in judgment. Furthermore, by contrasting real categorical *esse* (cause) with propositional *est* as the copula of truth (effect, Marietti nn. 895–896), Aquinas provides the exact textual warrant for Hoenen's and Bernard Lonergan's (*Verbum*, Ch. 2) insistence that judgment is not a mere juxtaposition of concepts, but a reflective intellectual posit affirming (or denying, as in diagonal commensurability) the correspondence between mental synthesis and objective necessity.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's dual analysis of diagonal incommensurability and the potential midpoint of a segment speaks directly to the symbolic foundations of *geometor.model*. In floating-point dynamic geometry software, commensurability and incommensurability are blurred into indistinguishable decimal approximations, obliterating the exact modal boundary that Aquinas highlights in Marietti n. 895. Because *geometor.model* represents every point, line, and circle in exact SymPy algebraic fields, the irrationality of √2 in a unit square or the golden ratio φ = (1 + √5)/2 in a golden section is preserved as an exact polynomial identity, allowing propositional queries over collinearity, concurrency, and commensurability to evaluate with strict Boolean truth. Likewise, before a bisecting circle-pair construction is executed in *geometor.model*, the midpoint of a segment exists only virtually—in potency—until explicit constructive steps reduce that point into actual algebraic coordinates within the model's directed acyclic graph.

section_notes.heading: Metaphysics Book VII, Lecture 10 — On Parts of the Form vs. Parts of Matter: Bronze Circle and Mathematical Circle in Intelligible Matter
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Expositing *Metaphysics* Z.10 (1034b20–1036a25), Aquinas brings crisp scholastic order to one of the most intricate chapters in the Aristotelian corpus. He introduces a fourfold distinction—form (*forma*), universal species (*quod quid erat esse* embracing common matter), concrete singular composite (*simul totum* in individual matter), and material parts—to resolve when parts precede or follow the whole. Most remarkably, in Marietti nn. 1494–1496, Aquinas harmonizes Aristotle's reference to singular mathematical circles (*circuli mathematici*) with *De Anima* III.5's enigmatic remark that the *intellectus passivus* is corruptible: mathematical singulars are grasped apart from external sensation by pure *phantasia* (here called *intellectus* or *intelligentia* by extension), proving against Platonic formalism that imagination supplies an inner spatial field (*materia intelligibilis*) capable of individuating multiple congruent lines and concentric or non-concentric circles of the exact same species.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Every geometric example in Lecture 10 illuminates the logical ordering of definitions in Euclid's *Elements* Book I. Aquinas's observation (Marietti n. 1483) that the acute angle is quantitatively part of the right angle yet posterior in definition reproduces *Elements* Book I, Definitions 10–12 verbatim: Euclid first defines the right angle via the equality of adjacent angles formed by a perpendicular straight line, and only subsequently defines the obtuse angle as greater than a right angle and the acute angle as *less than a right angle* (*angulus minor recto*). Similarly, *Elements* Book I, Definitions 15–18 define the circle first through the equidistance of its bounding line from one interior point, and only then define the diameter and the semicircle (*hemicyclium*) through the circle. Finally, Aquinas's appeal (Marietti n. 1494) to 'several equal lines and several similar figures' (*plures lineae aequales, et plures figurae similes*) captures the pervasive practice of Euclidean congruence and similarity proofs (Books I and VI), which compare two numerically distinct triangles or circles instantiating one identical universal definition.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: Hoenen explicitly cites *In VII Metaphysicorum*, lect. 10, Marietti n. 1496 alongside *Super Boetium De Trinitate* q. 5, a. 3, ad 3 in *De Noetica Geometriae*, Caput IV (§ 8, n. 2), to establish the ontological ground of geometric individuation and congruence. Matter is a principle of numerical multiplicity solely through presupposed dimensive quantity, upon whose removal substance remains indivisible. Because pure continuous extension (*continuum vel superficies vel corpus*) retains dimensive parts even when all sensible qualities (bronze, wood, temperature, color) are abstracted away, the geometer's imagination possesses an authentic *materia intelligibilis* in which numerically distinct figures of identical species can be constructed, superposed, and inspected. As Hoenen emphasizes, when a particular imagined circle 'recedes from actual inspection' (*abeuntes ab actu*, Marietti n. 1495), only the universal *ratio* remains in habitual intellect, explaining why actual geometric reasoning must continually reactivate determinate spatial phantasms.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Lecture 10's distinction between the universal definition of the circle and plural *circuli mathematici* individuated in *materia intelligibilis* mirrors the exact object model of *geometor.model* and *geometor.explorer*. In *geometor.model*, the universal algebraic form of a circle—the locus of points at a fixed squared radius *r²* from a center (*x₀*, *y₀*)—is instantiated as distinct symbolic *Circle* objects placed at distinct positions in the coordinate plane. Just as Aquinas proves in Marietti n. 1494 that geometry requires plural equal segments and plural circles of the same species to conduct demonstrations, constructive geometry in *geometor.model* begins from two initial points defining a unit segment and immediately instantiates two distinct congruent circles centered at each endpoint (Euclid I.1), while *geometor.explorer* renders those exact intelligible singulars on an SVG canvas for visual inspection.

section_notes.heading: Metaphysics Book VII, Lecture 11 — How Mathematical Species Are Defined Without Sensible Matter Yet Not Without Common Intelligible Matter
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: In *Metaphysics* Z.11 (1036a26–1037b7), Aquinas tracks Aristotle's polemic against two wings of the Old Academy: Platonists who collapsed mathematical objects directly into Ideal Numbers (identifying the straight line itself with the Dyad, probably Xenocrates) and those—including Plato himself and Speusippus—who posited *mathematica media* between Ideal Numbers and sensible bodies while still claiming the Dyad is the formal *species* of the line (Marietti nn. 1509–1511). Aquinas also identifies 'Socrates the Younger' (1036b25; cf. Plato's *Theaetetus* 147d and *Statesman* 257c) with Plato's literary persona of Socrates, diagnosing why his 'parable' misleads: because a circle can exist without bronze, Plato inferred that human nature can exist and be defined without flesh and bone, and academic hyper-abstractionists inferred further that triangles and circles can be defined without continuous lines! Aquinas restores hylomorphic proportion: lines stand to the triangle in common intelligible matter just as flesh and bone stand to man in common sensible matter.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Lecture 11 defends the irreducibility of geometric continuity against arithmetic reductionism—a foundational principle of Euclid's *Elements*, which treats continuous magnitude (Books I–VI, X–XIII) and discrete multitude (Books VII–IX) in distinct axiomatic books rather than reducing lines to pairs of points or triangles to the triad. In Marietti nn. 1508–1509, Aquinas notes that removing the continuous line from the definition of the triangle (bounded by three straight lines, *Elements* I, Def. 19) or the circle (bounded by one curved line, *Elements* I, Def. 15) leaves nothing save bare three-ness or oneness, obliterating spatial geometry altogether. Furthermore, in Marietti nn. 1520–1522 and 1529, Aquinas resolves why semicircles (*hemicycla*) never enter the definition of the universal circle even though letters enter the definition of a syllable: semicircles arise only by partitioning an individual circle's continuous extension, whereas common intelligible matter (a plane figure bounded by one line equidistant from a center) is essential to the universal species itself.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: For Hoenen (*De Noetica Geometriae*, Caput II and Caput IV), *Metaphysics* VII, lect. 11 delivers the decisive refutation of modern pure Hilbertian formalism avant la lettre. Just as the ancient Platonists sought to purge the continuum (*linea vel superficies*) from the essence of geometric figures so that only abstract numerical or relational multiplicities remained—with the fatal consequence remarked by Aquinas in Marietti n. 1512 that a triangle (three lines), a syllogism (three terms), and three-dimensional space would become formally isomorphic—modern formalist axiomatics replaces intuitive spatial content with uninterpreted 'transcendent terms' (*a*, *b*, *c*) satisfying purely syntactic postulates. Hoenen shows with Aquinas that while symbolic logic (*logica docens*) legitimately studies formal structures in abstraction, geometry itself cannot dispense with *materia intelligibilis communis*—the intuitively grasped continuum—without ceasing to be geometry.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's critique of reducing geometric figures to bare numerical counts illuminates a core architectural distinction in GEOMETOR between purely combinatorial graph structures and genuine constructive geometry in *geometor.model*. An abstract incidence triple of three elements could equally represent three terms in a syllogism or three nodes in a tree (*geometor.trees*), losing every metric and proportional invariant of Euclidean space. Because *geometor.model* embeds lines and circles within exact continuous algebraic geometry—retaining common intelligible matter through continuous quadratic and linear equations over symbolic coordinates—geometric figures preserve their intrinsic spatial curvature, incidence, and harmonic cross-ratios (*geometor.pappus*) rather than degenerating into uninterpreted combinatorial tokens.

section_notes.heading: Metaphysics Book IX, Lecture 3 — How the Name and Notion of Actuality Are Derived First from Sensible Motion
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Commenting on *Metaphysics* Θ.3–4 (1046b29–1047b30), Aquinas confronts the Megarian school (Eucleides of Megara and his followers, whom Aristotle names in 1046b29), who collapsed *dynamis* into *energeia* out of deterministic convictions. Aquinas sharpens Aristotle's four *reductiones ad absurdum*: Megarian actualism would mean an architect or geometer acquires and loses his habitual science every time he picks up or lays down his straightedge, sensible qualities collapse into Protagorean phenomenalism (*Metaphysics* Γ.5), animals turn blind and deaf dozens of times a day, and all becoming freezes into Eleatic immobility. Equally penetrating is Aquinas's commentary on modal logic in Θ.4 (Marietti nn. 1810–1814), carefully distinguishing contingency (*possibile* opposed to *necesse*) from broad possibility (*possibile* opposed to *impossibile*) to validate Aristotle's modal theorem—if *A* is possible and *A* necessarily implies *B*, then *B* is possible—and to correct misreadings of contraposition when an impossible antecedent implies a necessary consequent.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Aquinas twice invokes the touchstone theorem of Greek mathematical impossibility (Marietti nn. 1807–1808): the commensurability of the square's diagonal with its side. Whereas sitting or standing is contingently false at a given moment without entailing contradiction, supposing the diagonal commensurable with the side entails a formal impossibility—namely, as Aristotle notes in *Prior Analytics* I.23 (41a26–27) and as preserved in *Elements* X, Appendix 27, that one and the same integer would be simultaneously odd and even! Thus *reductio ad impossibile*—one of Euclid's primary engines of proof from *Elements* I.6 and I.7 onward through the method of exhaustion in Book XII—depends directly on the modal law demonstrated in Marietti nn. 1813–1814: when a posited geometric hypothesis (*A*) entails an impossible consequent (*B*, such as part equaling whole or odd equaling even), the hypothesis *A* is itself proved strictly impossible, not merely uninstantiated.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: Hoenen singles out Marietti nn. 1805–1806 twice in the Appendix to *De Noetica Geometriae* (citing p. 253 and pp. 270–271, indexed under concordance keys *aquinas:met:IX.3.1805* and *aquinas:met:9.3.1806*) as a master key to the epistemology of *actus* and *esse*. Quoting Aquinas verbatim—'since names are signs of intelligible conceptions, we first impose names upon those things which we first understand, *although they be posterior according to the order of nature*'—Hoenen shows how human cognition first grasps existential actuality in sensible *motus* (a fluent *esse* perceived directly in concrete experience, whence *moveri* is never attributed to non-beings, n. 1806) and then extends both the notion and the name *actus* upward to substantial form, intellectual operation, and finally *ipsum esse* itself, which is prior in nature though posterior in our reflective philosophical analysis.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Both the genetic primacy of motion and the preservation of habitual geometric potency in Lecture 3 resonate across the GEOMETOR ecosystem. In *geometor.explorer*, animated construction sequences bring geometric dependencies to life through visual motion—respecting Aquinas's psychological observation in Marietti n. 1805 that human intelligence most readily apprehends actuality through visible movement before abstracting timeless algebraic invariants. At the same time, in *geometor.elements* and *geometor.seer*, previously synthesized constructions and verified transformation rules persist as reusable habitual capabilities (active and cognitive *potentiae*), ready to be deployed across new problem instances without having to be re-learned from scratch at each invocation.

section_notes.heading: Metaphysics Book IX, Lecture 10 — On Discovering Geometric Truth by Dividing Figures in Act (Euclid I.32 and III.31)
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: In *Metaphysics* Θ.9 (1051a21–33), Aristotle compressed two famous geometric proofs into ten terse, elliptical Greek lines that baffled commentators from Alexander of Aphrodisias to pseudo-Alexander and Averroes. Aquinas's exposition in Marietti nn. 1888–1894 is a triumph of philosophical and mathematical clarity: situating Θ.9 as the transition from the ontological comparison of act and potency (in priority and goodness) to the veritative treatise of Θ.10, Aquinas explains *why* geometric discovery (*inventio*) depends upon actualizing potentiality. Because a continuous magnitude contains infinite potential divisions prior to actual construction, an undivided figure conceals the middle terms required for demonstration; when the geometer actively divides lines and surfaces (*facientes aliquid actu cognoscunt*), potential relations become actualized objects proportional to the intellect, which is itself act (*intellectus actus est*, n. 1894).
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Aquinas supplies full, crystal-clear reconstructions of both Euclidean theorems cited by Aristotle! First (Marietti nn. 1889–1890), for the theorem that a triangle's interior angles equal two right angles (*Elements* I.32), Aquinas produces base *AC* of triangle *ABC* continuously to form an exterior angle at *C*; invoking *Elements* I.13 (a straight line standing on a straight line makes two right angles or angles equal to two right angles) alongside the equality of the exterior angle to the two opposite interior angles (proved in Euclid via a parallel through *C* using I.29 and Postulate 2), the angle-sum theorem becomes immediately visible. Second (Marietti nn. 1891–1893), for Thales's theorem that every angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle (*Elements* III.31), Aquinas bisects diameter *AC* at center *D* and draws radius *DB*; because *DA*, *DC*, and *DB* are equal radii, triangles *DBA* and *DBC* are isosceles (*Elements* I.5), and by applying the exterior angle property (*Elements* I.32) to angles *BDC* and *ADB* at the center—whose sum equals two right angles (*Elements* I.13)—their sum is shown to be double the inscribed angle *ABC*, proving immediately that *ABC* is one right angle (a famously elegant pre-Euclidean variant of *Elements* III.31 preserved by Pappus and Eutocius!).
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: No single text in the Thomistic corpus better exemplifies the central thesis of Hoenen's *De Noetica Geometriae* and Bernard Lonergan's *Verbum: Word and Idea in Aquinas* (Ch. 1, opening with the celebrated Euclidean diagram insight!) than *In IX Metaphysicorum*, lect. 10, nn. 1888–1894 (cited by Hoenen under concordance key *aquinas:met:9.10.1894*). Look at Aquinas's repeated phrase in nn. 1890 and 1893: *statim manifestum fit videnti dispositionem figurae* ('it becomes immediately manifest to one seeing the disposition of the figure')! Neither blind sensory staring at an undivided triangle nor purely formal syllogizing without a diagram yields discovery; rather, heuristic imagination actively constructs auxiliary lines (*dividendo lineas et superficies*), and in that actualized spatial phantasm the agent intellect grasps the necessary formal nexus directly in act prior to formulating the demonstrative syllogism.
section_notes.geometor_significance: *In IX Metaphysicorum*, lect. 10 is the philosophical charter of the entire GEOMETOR project. In *geometor.model*, an initial seed configuration—such as two fundamental points—holds an immense lattice of harmonic ratios, golden sections, and regular polygons purely *in potentia*; as Aquinas writes in Marietti n. 1888, 'because in the first drawing of figures divisions of this sort exist in potency, what is sought does not immediately become manifest.' Every constructive step executed in *geometor.model*—extending a line through two points or describing a circle—literally performs Aquinas's *divisio reducit in actum quod erat in potentia*, computing exact symbolic polynomial intersections that bring latent points into actual existence. Once brought into act, *geometor.divine* immediately detects golden sections (φ) and harmonic ranges across collinear point-sets, while *geometor.explorer* renders the actualized *dispositio figurae* so the geometer sees the invariant structure directly in act.

section_notes.heading: Summa Theologiae I, q. 7, a. 1 & a. 3; q. 12, a. 4 — Being Itself as Most Formal of All; the Geometer's Infinite Line; Apprehending Absolute Being
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: In *Summa Theologiae* I, q. 7, a. 1 and 3, Aquinas transforms Aristotle's critique of the actual infinite (*Physics* III.4–8 and *De Caelo* I.5–7) by synthesizing it with Neoplatonic-Christian participation metaphysics (John Damascene and Pseudo-Dionysius). For the Presocratics and even for Aristotle, *to apeiron* carried the connotation of unfinished material indeterminacy—potency lacking terminating *peras* or form. Aquinas accepts Aristotle's hylomorphic premise for continuous magnitude—proving from natural place, diverging radii in circular rotation (*De Caelo* I.5, 271b26–272a7), and quantitative figure that no physical or mathematical body can be actually infinite—while inverting its metaphysical implication for pure form and *esse*: because form is contracted rather than perfected by matter, and *ipsum esse* is most formal of all (*maxime formale omnium*), subsistent *esse* unreceived in any limiting potency is supremely infinite and perfect.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Three foundational Euclidean doctrines converge in Question 7, Articles 1 and 3. First, Aquinas's principle that *figura* is the quantitative form consisting in the termination of magnitude (*q. 7, a. 1, ad 2* and *a. 3, co.*) directly quotes Euclid *Elements* Book I, Definition 14: *Figura est quae termino vel terminis continetur* ('A figure is that which is contained by any boundary or boundaries'). Second, Objection 1 and Reply 1 of Article 3 resolve a classic puzzle concerning Euclid's Postulate 2 ('To produce a finite straight line continuously in a straight line') and propositions such as *Elements* I.12 ('upon a given infinite straight line, from a given point which is not on it, to draw a perpendicular straight line') and I.22: following Aristotle (*Physics* III.7, 207b29–31), Aquinas explains that the geometer never assumes an actually infinite line, but calls a finite line 'infinite' (*indefinite*) insofar as it may be extended or cut off as far as any given construction requires. Third, Aquinas's geometric proof against infinite rotation (*a. 3, co.*) invokes the unbounded divergence of two rays drawn at an angle from a center.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: Hoenen explicitly cites *ST* I, q. 7, a. 1 (*illud quod est maxime formale omnium, est ipsum esse*, concordance key *aquinas:st:I.7.1*) and *ST* I, q. 12, a. 4, ad 3 (*intellectus noster potest in abstractione considerare id quod in concretione cognoscit*, concordance key *aquinas:st:I.12.4.ad3*) in the Appendix to *De Noetica Geometriae* (nn. 307, 410). For Hoenen, Question 12, Article 4, ad 3 supplies the decisive proof that human intelligence possesses a genuine, abstractive conception (*ratio essendi*) of *esse* itself—not merely concrete quiddities—through a 'certain resolution' (*per modum resolutionis cuiusdam*) analogous to its resolution of form from matter. Because the intellect resolves concrete beings into essence and existential act, it can formulate universal existential principles and recognize *esse* as the most formal perfection grounding every categorical mode of being, including quantitative extension.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's resolution of the *linea infinita geometrae* in *ST* I, q. 7, a. 3, ad 1 describes with uncanny exactitude how unbounded lines operate in *geometor.model* and *geometor.explorer*. In *geometor.model*, a *Line* constructed through two points is represented algebraically by homogeneous linear coefficients (*a*, *b*, *c*) satisfying *ax + by + c = 0*—not as a completed actual infinity of points, but as an indefinite rule of alignment capable of yielding exact finite intersections wherever another line or circle meets it, while *geometor.explorer* clips and renders that line across whatever finite bounding viewport the current construction demands. At the same time, Aquinas's theorem that every actual geometric figure is bounded by terminating limits (*figura*) underpins the finite, exact constructibility of polygons and polyhedra studied in *geometor.elements* and *geometor.pacioli*.

section_notes.heading: Summa Theologiae I, q. 84, a. 6–7 & q. 85, a. 1 — On the Origin of Science from Sensible Things, Turning to Phantasms, and Threefold Abstraction
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Written at the height of Aquinas's maturity (c. 1267–1268, contemporary with his *Sentencia libri De anima* in Part III of this Codex), Questions 84 and 85 orchestrate a grand historical dialectic among Democritus (*De Somno*, *De Generatione* I.8), Plato, Augustine (*83 Different Questions*, *De Genesi ad litteram* XII), Avicenna, and Aristotle (*De Anima* III.4–8, *Metaphysics* Z.10–11, *Posterior Analytics* II.19). By grounding human cognition in the substantial unity of the rational soul as *forma corporis*, Aquinas explains why our intellect occupies the exact ontological midpoint between bodily sense (bound to individual corporeal matter) and angelic intelligence (proportioned to separate forms): its proper object is the quiddity existing in corporeal matter, which must be abstracted from individuating conditions by the *intellectus agens* yet contemplated in concrete particulars via *conversio ad phantasmata*.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Question 85, Article 1, ad 2 codifies the epistemological charter of Euclidean geometry within the hierarchy of sciences: *numeri et dimensiones et figurae, quae sunt terminationes quantitatum*—precisely the subject-genera of Euclid's arithmetic (Books VII–IX), plane geometry (Books I–VI), and stereometry (Books XI–XIII)—can be considered apart from all sensible qualities (hot/cold, hard/soft) because dimensive quantity inheres in corporeal substance prior to sensible qualities, yet cannot be understood without substance subject to quantity (*materia intelligibilis communis*). Simultaneously, Question 84, Article 7's phenomenological appeal—that whenever we strive to understand or teach someone else, we form exemplary phantasms (*exempla*) in which to inspect the universal truth—describes the universal pedagogical structure of Euclid's *Elements*, where every general *protasis* ('In any triangle...') is immediately instantiated in a singular lettered *ekthesis* ('Let *ABC* be a triangle...').
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: Hoenen builds Chapters II and III of *De Noetica Geometriae* directly upon *ST* I, q. 84, a. 6 (and ad 3, concordance key *aquinas:st:I.q84.a6*), q. 84, a. 7, and q. 85, a. 1, ad 2 (concordance key *aquinas:st:I.85.1.ad2*), just as Lonergan centers *Verbum* Chapter 1 ('Insight into Phantasm') upon *ST* I, q. 84, a. 7! Hoenen emphasizes two revolutionary insights in these texts. First, because sensible cognition is only the *materia causae* while the *intellectus agens* supplies higher active power (*q. 84, a. 6, co. & ad 3*), intellectual judgment draws from defective sensible diagrams exact geometric limits—such as indivisible points and breadthless tangent lines (answering Protagoras's objection that sensible circles touch a ruler across a segment rather than at a single point)—that transcend raw sensory data while remaining objectively true of extended continua. Second, *q. 85, a. 1, ad 1–2* proves that geometric abstraction is an intuitive inspection of formal structure (*simplex et absoluta consideratio*) within *materia intelligibilis*, never a mendacious Platonic hypostatization.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's twin doctrines of *abstractio a materia sensibili* (*q. 85, a. 1, ad 2*) and *conversio ad phantasmata* (*q. 84, a. 7*) map directly onto the dual architecture pairing *geometor.model* with *geometor.explorer* (and, in abstract visual reasoning, *geometor.seer* with *geometor.seer_navigator*). *geometor.model* executes pure mathematical abstraction by stripping away every floating-point pixel artifact or physical imperfection, representing points, lines, and circles in exact algebraic species over *materia intelligibilis*; yet to comprehend, teach, and heuristically explore those symbolic structures, human reason requires *geometor.explorer*'s visual SVG diagrams—concrete exemplary phantasms (*per modum exemplorum*) in which the intellect directly beholds universal proportional harmonies instantiated in a particular construction.

section_notes.heading: Disputed Questions on the Power of God, q. 7, a. 2 — That Esse Is the Actuality of All Acts and the Perfection of All Perfections
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: *De Potentia* q. 7, a. 2 (disputed at Rome c. 1265–1266) represents Aquinas's most daring metaphysical synthesis, weaving together Aristotle (*Metaphysics* IV, V.7, *Posterior Analytics* I–II, *On Interpretation* I.1), Boethius (*De Hebdomadibus*), Hilary of Poitiers, Moses Maimonides (*Guide of the Perplexed* I.57), Pseudo-Dionysius (*De Divinis Nominibus* V), and the Neoplatonic *Liber de Causis* (Propositions 4, 8, and 9). Confronting Objection 9's Aristotelian-sounding claim that *esse* is the most indeterminate and imperfect substrate—analogous to prime matter awaiting categorical determination—Aquinas effects a profound metaphysical revolution: far from being minimal potency, *esse* is the ultimate act (*actualitas omnium actuum*) without which every substantial or accidental form remains merely potential in matter, in an agent's power, or in an intellect's concept, while finite essences contract *esse* as potency limits act.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: In Reply 11 (*ct_id* 60122), Aquinas anchors his crucial epistemological distinction between propositions self-evident in themselves (*per se notae secundum se*) and propositions self-evident to us (*quoad nos*) in Euclid's Fifth Common Notion (*Elements* Book I, Common Notion 5, cited via *Posterior Analytics* I.2): *Omne totum est maius sua parte* ('Every whole is greater than its part'). Because the predicate *greater than its part* is analytically contained in the intelligible *ratio* of a quantitative whole, anyone who grasps the geometric meaning of *totum* and *pars* immediately assents to the axiom once its terms are known (*cognitis terminis*); by contrast, although in God *esse* is identical with His essence, our intellect lacks direct quidditative vision of God's essence and must therefore demonstrate the propositional truth 'God is' (*an est*, Reply 1) from created effects.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: *De Potentia* q. 7, a. 2, ad 9 (concordance key *aquinas:de-potentia:7.2.ad9*) is the centerpiece of Hoenen's entire existential commentary in the Appendix to *De Noetica Geometriae* (cited four times across lines 303–362!). Hoenen subjects Aquinas's phrase *hoc quod dico esse* ('this that I call *esse*') to meticulous logico-noetic analysis: placed in the grammatical subject as a substantive infinitive (*Peri Hermeneias* I, lect. 5), *esse* signifies an authentic intellectual conception belonging to simple apprehension, drawn via resolution from concrete experience; yet when affirmed in the second operation of the mind, *esse* is posited as the existential act corresponding proportionally to each quidditative nature or relation—from permanent subsistent essences down to continuous spatial magnitudes and even the fluent, oscillatory *esse* of sound and light!
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's distinction in *De Potentia* q. 7, a. 2 between a form considered merely in potency or in conceptual definition versus a form posited in actual *esse* (ad 9)—paired with his distinction between *an est* as propositional verification and *quid est* as essential structure (ad 1 and ad 11)—illuminates the verification philosophy of GEOMETOR. Defining an abstract geometric ratio such as extreme and mean ratio (*Elements* VI, Def. 3) merely specifies *quid nominis* in thought; only when a rigorous compass-and-straightedge construction in *geometor.elements* or *geometor.model* actually brings the dividing point into existence—and *geometor.divine* verifies exact algebraic identity in act—is mathematical *esse* demonstratively established from first principles such as *Every whole is greater than its part*.

section_notes.heading: Disputed Questions on Truth, q. 10, a. 6 — Whether the Human Mind Receives Knowledge from Sensible Things and on First Indemonstrable Principles
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Disputed at Paris c. 1256–1259, *De Veritate* q. 10, a. 6 presents Aquinas's earliest comprehensive map of ancient and medieval epistemology, testing Aristotle's *De Anima* III.4–5 and *Posterior Analytics* I.18 and II.19 against nine formidable Augustinian, Boethian, and Avicennian objections. Particularly incisive is Objection 7's four-pronged dilemma arguing (via Avicenna's ontology of accidents) that an intelligible species can reside as mover neither in imagination, nor in the agent intellect, nor in the possible intellect, nor *per se*. Aquinas resolves the aporia in Reply 7 through his classic doctrine of dual causality: the *intellectus agens* acts as primary principal agent conferring actual immateriality, while the sensory phantasms act as secondary instrumental agents (*agens instrumentale vel secundarium*) conferring specific determination, so that the resulting species in the *intellectus possibilis* unites the formality of intellect with the objective content of sensible reality.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: The second *sed contra* (*ct_id* 53903) and the concluding synthesis of the *Responsio* (*ct_id* 53905) provide the genetic account of Euclid's Common Notions (*communes animi conceptiones* or *dignitates*): 'all our knowledge originally consists in the knowledge of first indemonstrable principles, and the knowledge of these arises in us from sense, as is clear at the end of the *Posterior Analytics*.' In geometry, universal conceptions such as *Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another* (Common Notion 1), *If equals be added to equals, the wholes are equal* (Common Notion 2), and *The whole is greater than the part* (Common Notion 5) are not innate Platonic memories prior to bodily experience, nor arbitrary conventions, but immediate intellectual insights ignited by the light of the *intellectus agens* the moment continuous wholes, parts, and equalities are presented in sensory and imaginative phantasms—principles within which all subsequent Euclidean theorems are virtually foreknown (*praecognoscimus in ipsis*).
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: Hoenen places *De Veritate* q. 10, a. 6, *sed contra* 2 (concordance key *aquinas:de-veritate:q10-a6*) at the very opening of Chapter IV of *De Noetica Geometriae* ('On the Origin of First Geometric Principles,' Caput IV, § 1; complementing his classic 1933 *Gregorianum* study *De origine primorum principiorum scientiae*). Commenting directly on Aquinas's thesis that all science originally consists in first indemonstrable principles arising from sense, Hoenen argues that elementary geometry's foundational axioms and postulates emerge from 'hidden'—that is, pre-reflective yet luminously conscious—operations that are simultaneously *abstractive* (drawing from the spatial phantasm as instrumental cause, Reply 7) and *intuitive* (immediately beholding the necessary formal nexus and exactitude of continuous boundaries by the light of the *intellectus agens* prior to deductive syllogizing).
section_notes.geometor_significance: *De Veritate* q. 10, a. 6 completes the epistemological circle of the Codex for both geometric exploration and machine reasoning in *geometor.seer*. Just as Aquinas rejects both pure apriorism (innate forms detached from sensory data) and passive empiricism (raw impressions devoid of active structural illumination) in favor of the synergy between instrumental phantasms and the active light of first principles, *geometor.seer* synthesizes verifiable Python transformation programs not by brute-force pixel memorization nor by ungrounded speculation, but by inspecting concrete visual grids (instrumental exemplars) through universal structural priors—symmetry, continuity, containment, and proportion—to abstract exact, necessary laws under which new particular instances are judged and foreknown.
